Time of Day Lighting Study: One Cabin, Four Moods

A lighting artist's job is not to make one pretty picture. It's to take a scene and make it read the way the moment needs: cold and quiet, bright and open, warm and nostalgic, or dark but still readable. So I set myself a simple exercise. One small scene, a log cabin by a pond in a pine forest, lit four times in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline (URP): Dawn, Noon, Dusk and Night.

I kept the rules tight on purpose. The main tools were the right ambient lighting and the directional light. On top of that I controlled the bounce lighting, the reflections and, where it helped, the colours of the materials themselves to get the look I wanted. The only extra lights are a few spot and area lights on the house, used as support lights so the cabin stands out in a render or a walk-through. No other artistic adjustments were made. Everything you see below comes from how the light is set up, not from a grade painted on afterwards.

The scene itself is a simple test scene with CC0 textures from Poly Haven. The lighting is the part I'm showing here. I rendered five cameras for each time of day, and the same cameras are used all the way through, so every comparison is like for like.

Two ideas carry the whole study. The first is that the sun and the sky are two different lights. The sun is one hard, directional key: it comes from one direction and casts sharp shadows. The sky is a huge soft light that wraps around everything and fills the shadows with its own colour. The second is that every lit surface becomes a light too. Sunlight that hits warm sand bounces back up and tints whatever is in shade. Getting the balance between those three, key, sky and bounce, right for each time of day is most of the work.

Dawn: the sky does the lighting

At dawn the sun is barely over the horizon. Its light travels through a lot of atmosphere, and the atmosphere scatters short blue wavelengths far more than long red ones (Rayleigh scattering). The result is a sky that is bright and blue while the direct sun is weak and warm. So at dawn the sky is the main light, and the directional light is a supporting player.

I set this up by letting the ambient lighting carry the scene with a cool blue, and keeping the directional light low and gentle so it gives shape without strong shadows. The shadows go blue because only the sky can reach them. That is real-world behaviour, and it's what sells the early morning feel. The warm lamp and porch light then sit against all that blue as the complementary accent, so the eye goes straight to the cabin.

Noon: hard key, strong bounce

Noon flips the balance. The sun is high and close to white, so the directional light becomes the dominant key. Shadows are short, dark-edged and sit right under things, and the sky turns into fill: it lifts the shadow side with a light blue.

The thing that makes noon look right, or wrong, is bounce. A bright sandy clearing in full sun reflects a lot of light back up into the porch, under the eaves and through the windows. If that bounce is too weak the shade looks like a black hole. Too strong and the image looks flat and washed out. So I tuned how much indirect light the scene gets and kept an eye on the material colours, because the colour of a surface decides how much light, and what colour of light, it sends back.

Dusk: warm key, long shadows

At dusk the sun is low again, but this time the scene is meant to feel warm, not cold. The sunlight now passes through even more atmosphere, so it arrives orange, and the sky near the sun picks up that warmth. The low angle stretches the shadows across the clearing, which adds a lot of depth and gives the image strong leading lines towards the cabin.

For dusk I pushed the directional light warm and low and let the ambient pick up warmth too, so the shadows stay rich rather than going cold. Inside the cabin I controlled the bounce directly. You can see it in the editor capture below: orange area lights lying on the floor exactly where the sun patches fall, so the light that "bounces" off those patches carries the same warm colour into the room.

Reflections matter just as much as the lights. The pond and anything glossy show you the sky, so if the sky colour changes and the reflections don't, the water looks pasted in. At a low viewing angle water is mostly a mirror, which is why the pond is such a strong read of the time of day in every shot.

Night: support lights carry the image

Night is where the rule about support lights earns its keep. With only a dim, cool ambient and the moon as the key, the cabin and the forest end up at almost the same brightness, and the house disappears into the trees. Moonlight is just reflected sunlight, but in low light our eyes see it as blue, so the ambient goes cool and dark while the roof catches a cool moonlit edge.

This is where separation comes in. Spot lights on the facade, area lights glowing at the windows and the lamp post's pool of light on the ground lift the cabin away from the background. The warm-cool contrast does the rest: warm practical light against a cool night reads instantly as "someone lives here".

Four moods, one scene

Here is the same camera across all four. Nothing changed in the scene between them except the lighting setup described above.

What I took away

The biggest lesson is how far you can get with just two lights and good control over the indirect. The directional light and the ambient set the time of day. Bounce and reflections make it believable. Material colours decide how much of that light comes back. Support lights are there to guide the eye, not to fix the lighting, and if a scene needs a lot of them, the base setup is usually wrong.

  • Start from the sky, not the sun. At dawn and night the ambient is the image. At noon it is the fill.
  • Treat bounce as a light you design. Where the sun lands, light comes back with that surface's colour, so place and colour it on purpose.
  • Keep reflections in step with the sky. Water and gloss give away a mismatch straight away.
  • Use support lights for separation. A few spot and area lights on the hero asset are enough to make it read, especially at night.
  • Earn the mood with light. No grade on top means every choice above has to work on its own.

If you're interested in the technical side of lighting, I also wrote about a voxel light baker for streamed VR scenes. I'm a Technical Artist and Unity engineer with 6+ years of experience, based in Dubai, and lighting is the part of the job I enjoy most. Textures in this scene are CC0 from Poly Haven.
